elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that this is a systematic review and describes its aim.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a clear statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature, non-English language studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were excluded from the search.
elements.reason: The abstract lists multiple exclusion criteria but does not explicitly state the main inclusion criteria in the abstract (only implied by the review aim).

elements.quote: a comprehensive search across PubMed and Embase databases was performed of peer-reviewed literature published from inception until June 2024.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources (PubMed and Embase) and reports the date range/last search (until June 2024).
The abstract does not report any methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.
The abstract does not specify the methods used to present and synthesize results (e.g., narrative synthesis or meta-analysis) within the abstract text.

elements.quote: The search yielded 2950 records, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria. The studies were carried out mainly in countries in Africa (53.3%)... The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (15) and summarizes key study characteristics, but does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%). The methods used for estimating health benefits were compartmental models (40.0%), individual-based models (40.0%), static models (13.0%) and linear regression model (7%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results summarizing intervention use and model types (and number of studies in percentages) but does not present outcome effect estimates or participant numbers per outcome.
No meta-analysis was conducted or reported in the abstract or provided evidence, so reporting a summary estimate and interval is not applicable.
The review does not report comparative group effect directions in the abstract (no group comparisons/meta-analysis), so this item is not applicable.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization, the use of country-specific epidemiological and cost data in performing modelling analyses, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results. It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for fairness and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and states important implications and recommendations.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.reason: The abstract (or front matter) provides the registry name (PROSPERO) and the registration number.

elements.quote: There is limited evidence in peer-reviewed literature on modelling for malaria optimization in limited resource settings. The country focus of the modelling studies included in the review were not representative of the burden of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. ... The limited number of modelling analyses for malaria control optimization specific to countries within Africa and Asia is as a consequence of the lack or inaccessibility of country-specific epidemiologic and cost data at the national and subnational levels. This data gap limits future studies within the respective countries, limits the build-up of a critical mass of modellers within these countries, and makes it challenging for policymakers to make an evidence-based informed case to potential donors for future funding.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge and highlights important uncertainties and data gaps (limited evidence, lack of country-specific data, representativeness issues).

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract states the importance of modelling for decision-making under constrained budgets and explicitly explains the need and objectives of the review.

No evidence was found describing existing similar systematic reviews or explaining the need for the current review as an update/replication; no prior review citations or discussion were provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The review focuses on models for optimization of malaria control rather than on estimating effects of specific interventions; therefore describing mechanisms of action of interventions is not applicable to this review's primary aim.

elements.quote: All studies investigated WHO-recommended interventions for control or elimination targets (Table 2), such as insecticide-treated nets [10, 11, 16-18, 25, 28, 29, 33-38], seasonal malaria chemoprevention [16, 18, 25, 28, 33, 37], intermittent preventive treatment [16, 25, 28, 37, 38], indoor residual spraying [16-18, 28, 29, 32-38], mass drug administration [16, 18, 29], and diagnosis and treatment through community health workers or health facilities [10, 11, 25, 28, 29, 32, 35-38].
elements.reason: Although the review addresses multiple interventions and contexts (so a logic model could be applicable), no evidence was found that a logic model or similar hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes was presented.

elements.quote: 'The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.'
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the review research question and the main aim to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization and to assess their strengths and limitations.

elements.quote: 'The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.'
elements.reason: The review's stated objective focuses on identifying and characterizing models for resource allocation rather than on comparing intervention effects; it does not present planned comparisons in PICO format, so the PICO-style comparison requirement for intervention-effect reviews does not apply.

elements.quote: Each record in the search were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024; (3) Studies were included irrespective of the targeted geographical regions; (4) Studies were included irrespective of the population subgroups; (5) Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: The text lists specific study characteristics used to determine eligibility including language, publication date, geographic scope, population, model type, Plasmodium species, number of interventions, use of cost data, and outcomes.

elements.quote: A total of 15 articles on models for malaria control optimization were identified from the literature. The majority of modelling analyses focused on countries in Africa and in the Asia Pacific regions. The interventions most commonly found in the analyses were ITNs, IRS, SMC and improved clinical case management. The data sources were country specific for some of the studies, although all studies had to rely on non-country-specific data to complete the analysis. The administrative level of analysis was at both the national and subnational levels, with a few studies having only subnational data analysis. There was a significant number of studies that had a budget constraint. However, very few carried out resource allocation within their constrained budgets. The studies included in this review exhibit various strengths and limitations, which will be outlined and examined below.
elements.reason: The discussion summarizes and characterises the review's findings (geographic focus, common interventions, data sources, analysis levels and budget constraints), which is partial contextual interpretation of results. However, it does not explicitly compare or place these findings against external evidence beyond the included studies (e.g., other published reviews or broader literature), so the requirement to 'interpret the results in the context of other evidence' is only partially met.
